findings.headline: Government has adopted the 'One East Sussex' proposals, with East Sussex County Council to cease to exist and merge with the five borough and district councils, and one strategic authority coming into being in 2028
findings.detail: The paper says the administering authority for the LGPS in East Sussex will be replaced by one strategic authority. It lists merging notional assets and liabilities of the defunct councils among the changes the fund must respond to.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation that abolishes a county council and its pension fund's administering authority is a structural change that finance directors and lenders in other areas will watch.
findings.figures: Five borough and district councils; new strategic authority coming into being in 2028
findings.quote: will cease to exist, merging with the five borough and district councils that are currently in place in the county.

findings.headline: Fund must adopt a Senior LGPS Officer role by 31 December 2026, which the Section 151 Officer cannot hold
findings.detail: Fit for the Future legislation created the role, which will be responsible for all aspects of managing the LGPS within the administering authority. The paper says arrangements to separate it from the Section 151 Officer role are ongoing.
findings.matters: The requirement that a council's section 151 officer cannot also run the pension fund affects how finance directors allocate responsibilities, and the deadline is one other councils must also meet.
findings.figures: Deadline of 31 December 2026
findings.quote: the recent Fit for the Future legislation created a new role that will need to be adopted by the Fund by 31 December 2026 – the Senior LGPS Officer.

findings.headline: Pension Committee put on hold material investment strategy changes, delaying allocation to parts of the illiquid asset portfolio
findings.detail: The Pension Committee paused material strategy changes because of uncertainty around pooling. The delay means the fund has not yet brought illiquid asset holdings back up to target benchmark weights.
findings.matters: Delayed rebalancing into illiquid assets shows how pooling transition can hold back planned allocations, a pressure other funds in the same position may face.
findings.figures: Not stated in the paper
findings.quote: most notably delaying allocation to parts of the illiquid asset portfolio to bring the Fund back up to targeted benchmark weights.

findings.headline: Fund's assets total £5.3bn at 31 March 2026, of which £3.6bn was invested in pooled funds with ACCESS, and the fund became a shareholder in Border to Coast from 1 April 2026
findings.detail: The paper reports that the government did not support the ACCESS pool's proposal, so the fund moved to Border to Coast Pension Partnership. Wind-down of ACCESS will take some time, with the priority being the safe and efficient transfer of assets.
findings.matters: Pool transitions of this size move billions of pension assets between structures and carry transfer and wind-down risk, which other funds and lenders to councils will track as the pool landscape changes.
findings.figures: £5.3bn total fund assets; £3.6bn invested in pooled funds with ACCESS; 1 April 2026 pool shareholding date
findings.quote: The Fund also became a shareholder in its new pooling partner, Border to Coast Pension Partnership, on 1 April 2026.

findings.headline: Fund expects to become increasingly cashflow negative in coming years as employer contribution rates fall and pensions in payment rise
findings.detail: The paper says the fund was already cashflow negative from member activities. It links the expected worsening to lower employer contribution rates and the high inflation uplift applied to pensions in payment in recent years. It says the fund will focus on income when setting strategy.
findings.matters: A pension fund moving to sustained cashflow deficit changes how it funds benefit payments from investment income and assets, which is relevant to councils treating the fund as a long-term funding source.
findings.figures: Pension increases for the year were 1.7% down from 6.7% and 10.1% in the preceding two years
findings.quote: the reduction in employer contribution rates will mean that the Fund will become increasingly cashflow negative in the coming years.

findings.headline: Fund re-affirmed a funding level of 117% as at 31 March 2025 after the triennial valuation, with most employers' contribution rates falling
findings.detail: The triennial valuation was completed over the year and an updated Funding Strategy Statement was to be in place by 31 March 2026. The paper says the majority of employers saw a fall in contribution rates.
findings.matters: Employer contribution rates set by the valuation determine the cash the fund receives from every participating council, which matters to finance directors budgeting employer costs.
findings.figures: 117% funding level as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Fund re-affirmed a strong funding level of 117% as at 31March 2025 and the majority of the Fund’s employers saw a fall in contribution rates.

findings.headline: Fund investment return of 6.1% for the year to 31 March 2026, against an underperformance of 4.5% relative to benchmark
findings.detail: The paper reports a positive investment return for the year but a shortfall against the benchmark. It attributes the gap to growth, quality and sustainability-oriented equity mandates, and to impact and ESG mandates constrained by sector exclusions.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can compare this shortfall with their own pension exposure and the investment assumptions behind their contribution rates.
findings.figures: 6.1% investment return; 4.5% underperformance against benchmark
findings.quote: The investment return for the year to 31 March 2026 was a positive 6.1%, however when compared to the benchmark, this was an underperformance of 4.5%.

findings.headline: The proposed 2025/26 audit fee is £115,493 excluding VAT, against £101,515 for 2024/25, after fee variations for triennial valuation data testing and Oracle migration work.
findings.detail: The total comprises the PSAA scale fee of £108,479 plus variations of £5,000 for triennial valuation data testing and £2,014 for the Oracle implementation. Non-audit IAS 19 letter fees of £2,500 bring total fees to Grant Thornton to £117,993.
findings.matters: Finance directors comparing external audit costs across councils and pension funds would want the size of the increase and the variations driving it.
findings.figures: £115,493 total audit fee (exc. VAT); £101,515 prior year; £108,479 PSAA scale fee; £5,000 and £2,014 fee variations; £117,993 total fees
findings.quote: Total audit fee (Exc. VAT) 115,493 101,515

findings.headline: The auditor reports that the migration of fund ledger balances from SAP to Oracle was complete and that no accuracy issues were found in the transferred data.
findings.detail: Key finance data moved from SAP to Oracle at the start of 2025/26, and all year transactions were recorded on Oracle. The auditor's IT specialists assisted with the data migration testing, and the auditor carried out completeness and accuracy reconciliations between the two systems.
findings.matters: The auditor's conclusion on a ledger migration is a reference point for finance teams at other councils planning or running the same kind of system change.
findings.quote: We have reviewed and tested the reconciliation of balances from the SAP system onto the Oracle Ledger and are satisfied that the transfer was complete.

findings.headline: The auditor raised a medium-rated recommendation on £445k of reconciling items in the bank reconciliation, which management links to the SAP-to-Oracle migration.
findings.detail: The auditor could not readily identify a complete population of genuine reconciling items at year end, because several balances in the listed account codes were not genuine timing differences. The auditor judged the residual difference trivial, and management reports a root cause fix and a dedicated reconciliation process for account 87104.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council moving ledgers would want to see how reconciliation controls were affected by a system change, including manual intervention on payments processed through Altair.
findings.figures: £445k reconciling items; Medium rating
findings.quote: Within our cash testing, we challenged management regarding the nature of the £445k of reconciling items identified within the bank reconciliation.

findings.headline: Note 26 disclosed outstanding capital commitments of £246.2m, against an independently verified total of £220.1m, and management agreed to amend the note.
findings.detail: The auditor found the disclosed figure was an output error inconsistent with the supporting workings. The auditor treated the difference as non-trivial and recommended the note be updated, and management agreed.
findings.matters: A disclosed commitment figure overstated by about £26m is a reporting error that finance teams and lenders reading pension fund commitments would want to see corrected.
findings.figures: £246.2m disclosed; £220.1m independently verified; £26.1m difference
findings.quote: The disclosure for outstanding capital commitments within Note 26 states a balance of £246.2m.

findings.headline: The auditor identified a circa £6.2m understatement of Level 3 investment valuations at 31 March 2026, which management is not proposing to adjust.
findings.detail: The misstatement arose from timing, because investment manager valuations updated after the draft accounts were circulated. Management proposes leaving the financial statements unchanged on the basis that the difference is immaterial, and the Audit Committee is to confirm this through the Letter of Representation.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know that unadjusted Level 3 valuation differences are being carried in the accounts, and that the auditor treats the cause as common across LGPS funds.
findings.figures: circa £6.2 million understatement; £6,168k net understatement of Level 3 investments; £1.15 billion Level 3 investments balance; £5,280,556k total net assets per final accounts
findings.quote: Management are proposing not to amend the financial statements on the basis that the differences are not material both quantitatively and qualitatively.

findings.headline: One employer remains to be onboarded to i-Connect, with the Fund working with its new payroll software provider ahead of the next Annual Benefit Statement cycle.
findings.detail: Fortnightly progress calls are in place with the remaining employer. Officers are also working on payroll changes, academy conversions and TUPE transfers that affect i-Connect data readiness.
findings.matters: Payroll-driven data feeds to pension funds are a shared operational dependency, and academy and TUPE churn affects other councils' employer lists too.
findings.figures: 1 employer remaining
findings.quote: Only one employer remains to be on-boarded

findings.headline: Survivors' pension and death grant records still to be reviewed under the April 2026 regulation changes number 2,400+ and 77, with a proposed deadline of 31 January 2028.
findings.detail: The Team is working with pension software suppliers to identify cases in scope for the April 2026 regulation changes. The paper says not all the records will require amendments, and the figures are still being refined.
findings.matters: A large retrospective review with a deadline roughly 15 months out is a remediation workload that other funds facing the same regulations will also have to scope.
findings.figures: 2,400+ survivors' pensions; 77 death grants; deadline 31 January 2028
findings.quote: 2,400+ survivors’ pensions and 77 death grants

findings.headline: The 2025/26 Annual Allowance calculations and letters were issued before the 06 October 2026 statutory deadline, after 300+ potential cases were reduced to 58.
findings.detail: Officers identified 300+ potential cases in August 2026, and 250+ were descoped at the data collection stage. The 58 remaining cases were calculated and letters issued before the deadline, with 6 showing tax payable.
findings.matters: A statutory deadline met on a scoped-down case list is a concrete example of how a fund handles a late-identified regulatory exercise.
findings.figures: 300+ potential cases; 250+ descoped; 58 remaining cases; 25 PIA under £60k; 27 PIA exceeded with no tax due; 6 PIA exceeded with tax payable; AA limit £60k; deadline 06 October 2026
findings.quote: All the necessary calculations and letters were issued before the statutory deadline 06 October 2026.

findings.headline: The Pension Administration Team is carrying 4 vacancies and is recruiting 2 Pensions Administrators after one resignation.
findings.detail: A Pensions Administrator resigned and moved to another position within the Council, so the Team is seeking to recruit 2 Pensions Administrators. The paper says the Team is currently carrying 4 vacancies.
findings.matters: Vacancies in a small in-house administration team are a staffing constraint that other councils running their own pension administration will recognise.
findings.figures: 4 vacancies; 2 Pensions Administrators being recruited
findings.quote: The team is currently carrying 4 vacancies.

findings.headline: The Pension Administration Team completed 97.9% of July to September 2026 work within service level, against 97.6% in April to June 2026.
findings.detail: The Team processed 97.9% of completed work within the applicable service level in Q3 2026. The paper's summary table shows Q2 2026 at 97.6%, with 118 tasks outside SLA in Q3 against 122 in Q2.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing administration cost or service quality across councils has a measured on-time rate for a fund-run team to benchmark against.
findings.quote: The Pension Administration Team processed 97.9% of completed work within the applicable service level during July to September 2026

findings.headline: The Pension Fund's budget for 2026/27 was approved at £100,000 at the March 2026 Joint Committee, and then increased after the Fund joined the pool
findings.detail: The Joint Committee approved a £100,000 budget for 2026/27 before the Fund joined Border to Coast. The budget was raised because the partnership expanded to 18 Partner Funds and a larger external venue is needed. The report says the budget is indicative and partners are recharged only final actual costs.
findings.matters: Funds joining a pool must budget for shared running costs that are only indicative until the final recharge, which other finance officers will also face.
findings.figures: £100,000; 18 Partner Funds
findings.quote: a budget of £100,000 was approved for 2026/27.

findings.headline: The Head of Pensions is proposed to take the new Senior LGPS Officer role, separate from the Section 151 Officer, subject to constitutional changes
findings.detail: The regulations require a Senior LGPS Officer role, separate from the Section 151 Officer, within six months of 30 June 2026. The report says the Head of Pensions will take the role once the Governance Committee recommends constitutional changes and Full Council agrees them. A separate report on the agenda covers how the role relates to the Chief Finance Officer.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will need to decide how to split responsibilities between the S151 Officer and a new pensions senior officer.
findings.figures: within 6 months following 30 June 2026
findings.quote: the Head of Pensions will assume the role of Senior Officer for the Fund.

findings.headline: The Fund's Independent Person appointment is due before 31 December 2026, with contracts being agreed after a preferred candidate was selected
findings.detail: The report says the Fund must appoint an Independent Person within six months of 30 June 2026. Interviews were held and a preferred candidate identified, and officers are now agreeing contracts. The stated completion date is before 31 December 2026.
findings.matters: This is a statutory governance deadline under the new regulations that other funds must also meet.
findings.figures: within 6 months following 30 June 2026; before 31 December 2026
findings.quote: work is underway to agree contracts and finalise the appointment before 31 December 2026.

findings.headline: The Power of Attorney documentation for Border to Coast is the one document still outstanding, with signing anticipated in December 2026 or early 2027
findings.detail: The report says all other documentation for joining the pool, including the Investment Management Agreement, has been executed. The Power of Attorney gives the pool oversight and execution of the Fund's assets. The report expects signing in December 2026 or early 2027.
findings.matters: The Power of Attorney gives the pool control over the fund's assets, so its signing date is a condition on the transition for any council in the same position.
findings.figures: December 2026; early 2027
findings.quote: It is anticipated this will be signed in December 2026 or early 2027.

findings.headline: Border to Coast expects to deliver full investment management services to the Fund from April 2027, with the Investment Strategy Statement finalised in February 2027
findings.detail: The report says Border to Coast expects to provide asset allocation and investment advisory services from April 2027. The Fund's Investment Strategy Statement is expected to be finalised in February 2027. Hymans Robertson will remain investment adviser until the pool provides full advisory services.
findings.matters: The date ties the pool's service start to the Fund's strategy document, which matters to any council planning its own pool transition.
findings.figures: April 2027; February 2027
findings.quote: are expected to be delivered to the Fund from April 2027.

findings.headline: The Fund remains invested in ACCESS pooled investment funds, with asset transfers to Border to Coast still to be completed
findings.detail: The report says reorganising the Fund's assets will take some time because it must be assessed across all partner funds. The Fund will stay in ACCESS funds until transfers are completed, and the report gives no transfer date.
findings.matters: Finance officers at peer funds moving between pools will want to know how long dual arrangements and asset transfers take in practice.
findings.quote: the Fund will remain invested in ACCESS pooled investment funds until transfers are completed.

findings.headline: East Sussex Pension Fund became a member of Border to Coast Pensions Partnership Ltd Pool on 1 April 2026, after government did not support the ACCESS pool's proposal
findings.detail: The report says government decided not to support the ACCESS pool's proposal under the Fit for the Future consultation. Officers then identified Border to Coast as the new pooling partner, and the Fund joined on 1 April 2026. The Joint Committee membership has since grown to 18 Partner Funds.
findings.matters: A finance director at another fund that has to change pools under Fit for the Future can compare this route and timetable with their own.
findings.figures: 1 April 2026; 18 Partner Funds
findings.quote: the Fund became a member of that pool on 1 April 2026.

findings.headline: The Chief Finance Officer keeps section 151 responsibilities for the whole council while the Pension Fund leadership role moves out
findings.detail: The report states that the Chief Finance Officer will continue to hold the council's statutory section 151 duties. The paper says the officer will still give independent financial oversight of the Pension Fund and advice to the Pension Committee and Pension Board. It also says pension-related duties such as signing the pension fund statement of accounts can remain with the Chief Finance Officer.
findings.matters: It shows how a finance director's pension oversight role can continue after the Senior Officer role is separated, which other councils will need to decide for themselves.
findings.quote: The Chief Finance Officer will continue to discharge the Council’s statutory responsibilities under section 151 of the Local Government Act 1972.

findings.headline: East Sussex proposes that the Head of Pensions become LGPS Senior Officer, removing that role from the Chief Finance Officer
findings.detail: The report says the new regulations require the LGPS Senior Officer to be a different person from the section 151 officer. The proposal moves day-to-day leadership of the Pension Fund, including implementation of strategies, administration, investments, and risk escalation, to the Head of Pensions. The paper asks the Pension Board to comment before it goes to the Pension Committee and the Governance Committee.
findings.matters: Any council with a pension fund will need the same separation under the 2026 regulations, so finance directors can compare how East Sussex splits the two roles.
findings.quote: For the East Sussex Pension Fund, it is proposed that the Head of Pensions holds the role of LGPS Senior Officer and removes these responsibilities from the Chief Finance Officer.

findings.headline: Fund Officer costs are forecast £98k below budget, due mainly to vacancies in the Pensions Administration and Governance teams
findings.detail: The paper links the staff underspend to vacancies in two teams. It says those vacancies, together with a lower rate charged by East Sussex County Council, also contribute to a £45k forecast reduction in overheads.
findings.matters: Vacancy savings are offsetting non-staff pressures in this budget, and a finance director can compare this with how other funds are managing staffing against pooling and regulatory workload.
findings.figures: £98k forecast below budget on Fund Officers; £45k forecast reduction in overheads
findings.quote: Fund Officer costs are forecast to be £98,000 below budget, primarily due to vacancies within the Pensions Administration and Governance teams.

findings.headline: Border to Coast investment and data platform project adds £0.250m to investment advice costs, against a budget that did not include it
findings.detail: The paper says the additional Border to Coast charges relate to a project to enhance its investment and data platform to meet the Pension Schemes Act requirements. It says these costs were not known when the budget was set. The investment advice line is forecast at a £219k overspend after a £15k saving from ending independent adviser costs and a £16k reprofiling to governance.
findings.matters: Pooling-vehicle charges for legislative compliance projects are a cost that other pool members in the same position may also see, and it shows how pool-level decisions flow into a single fund's budget.
findings.figures: £0.250m above budget for Border to Coast; £219k forecast overspend on investment advice; £15k saving from ending independent adviser costs; £16k reprofiled to governance
findings.quote: Border to Coast Pensions Partnership Ltd (Border to Coast) costs are £0.250m above budget, reflecting additional charges for a project to enhance its investment and data platform to meet the requirements of the Pension Schemes Act.

findings.headline: East Sussex Pension Fund forecasts 2026/27 outturn of £5.705m against a £5.503m budget, an increase of £0.202m
findings.detail: The forecast overspend is attributed mainly to higher investment advice, IT systems licences and hardware, admin operational support and improvement projects. It is partly offset by savings in Fund Officer costs, overheads and consultancy.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the size and drivers of this Q2 overspend on a pension fund administration budget with the pressures other administering authorities are reporting.

findings.headline: Capital programme borrowing requirement increased by £2.136m from the February 2026 forecast to £141.558m.
findings.detail: The revised Q1 forecast for borrowing driven by the capital programme is £141.558m, compared to the February 2026 estimate of £139.422m. Total CFR-driven borrowing (including a £70.000m capitalisation direction) is forecast at £211.558m, up from £209.422m. The paper does not detail the causes of this increase in the capital forecast.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders track whether councils deliver capital plans within approved budgets; this variance from the February forecast signals scope growth or cost inflation that will require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: New borrowing requirement £211.558m (revised forecast) vs £209.422m (February estimate); capital programme element £141.558m vs £139.422m
findings.quote: The total CFR is expected to give rise to a new borrowing requirement of £211.558m (£141.558m capital programme and £70.000m capitalisation direction) by the end of the year, compared to the original estimate of requirement of £209.422m (£139.422m capital programme and £70.000m capitalisation direction).

findings.headline: Cash investment balances fell 52% in one year, from £137.2m to £65.5m, as the council draws down reserves to fund the capital programme and avoid new borrowing at elevated rates.
findings.detail: The council is deliberately using internal cash reserves rather than incurring new debt during a period of high interest rates. This represents a strategic choice to manage borrowing costs, but indicates that liquid financial resources are declining significantly. The paper notes the council has £75.000m of internal borrowing (reserves) available to support 2026/27 capital spending, with new external borrowing expected to fund the remainder.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial resilience would be concerned about the rapid depletion of liquid reserves, while peer finance directors would track this as a response to rate pressure and question whether this rate of reserve use is sustainable.
findings.figures: Opening cash £137.2m (Q1 2025/26), closing £65.5m (Q1 2026/27); 52% reduction
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 30 June 2026 have fallen by 52% in one year, from £137.2m at Q1 2025/26 to £65.5m due to continued use of cash balances to support the capital programme and revenue cashflow requirements whilst new borrowing is delayed during a time of elevated rates.

findings.headline: Investment management is delivering above-benchmark returns despite cash position constraints, demonstrating competent treasury execution under stress.
findings.detail: Q1 average investment return of 4.01% exceeded the SONIA benchmark of 3.73% by 28 basis points. Investment risk exposure (0.004–0.005%) remains far below the strategy's allowable limit of 0.050%, indicating disciplined credit quality management. This performance is achieved while managing a falling and constrained portfolio.
findings.matters: Strong treasury management during a period of cash depletion and liquidity pressure demonstrates financial discipline and capability, which supports lender confidence in the council's ability to manage large external borrowing programmes.
findings.figures: Investment return 4.01% vs 3.73% SONIA (+28 basis points); investment risk 0.004–0.005% vs 0.050% limit
findings.quote: The average investment return over Q1 was 4.01% performing above the benchmark rate by 28 basis points (or 0.28 percentage points).

findings.headline: Council expects to require £136.558m in new external borrowing during 2026/27, to be raised after exhausting £75.000m of internal resources.
findings.detail: The strategy allocates £75.000m of internal borrowing (reserves and temporary working capital) towards the capital and capitalisation programmes. This leaves £136.558m that must be raised from external debt markets. The timing of this borrowing will be managed in relation to treasury strategy and economic conditions.
findings.matters: A borrowing requirement of this scale and imminence will determine the council's market access and cost of capital, directly affecting whether it can proceed with capital plans; the wording about timing suggests borrowing may be deferred if rates remain high.
findings.figures: £136.558m new external borrowing; £75.000m internal borrowing; £211.558m total 2026/27 borrowing requirement
findings.quote: It is therefore expected that new borrowing of £136.558m may be required to support the capital programme and capitalisation direction during 2026/27, although the timing of actual borrowing will be considered in the context of the wider treasury management position and underlying economic environment.

findings.headline: Capital programme costs have increased above original forecast, raising total external borrowing requirement by £2.136m to £211.558m.
findings.detail: Capital programme CFR closing balance revised upward from £334.064m to £339.700m. Capital programme borrowing requirement increased from £30.008m original estimate to £33.344m revised forecast. Total new borrowing requirement now £211.558m against original estimate of £209.422m.
findings.matters: Cost overruns mean larger funding gaps; combined with depleting cash reserves, the council has less flexibility to absorb further programme pressures or delays in accessing debt markets.
findings.figures: Capital programme CFR £334.064m to £339.700m; capital borrowing requirement £30.008m to £33.344m; total borrowing need £211.558m vs £209.422m forecast
findings.quote: The total CFR is expected to give rise to a new borrowing requirement of £211.558m (£141.558m capital programme and £70.000m capitalisation direction) by the end of the year, compared to the original estimate of requirement of £209.422m (£139.422m capital programme and £70.000m capitalisation direction).

findings.headline: Cash investment balances have fallen 52% in one year to £65.5m as the council uses reserves to fund capital and revenue spending while delaying new borrowing.
findings.detail: Balances fell from £137.2m in Q1 2025/26 to £65.5m in Q1 2026/27. The council is using cash reserves to support capital programme and revenue spending rather than accessing debt markets, a deliberate strategy given current interest rates. A £2.0m PWLB loan at 7.125% matured during the quarter.
findings.matters: Rapidly shrinking liquidity cushion means the council will be forced to enter debt markets for substantial sums within months, reducing flexibility to time borrowing decisions or manage market windows.
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 30 June 2026 have fallen by 52% in one year, from £137.2m at Q1 2025/26 to £65.5m due to continued use of cash balances to support the capital programme and revenue cashflow requirements whilst new borrowing is delayed during a time of elevated rates.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report PTBs and ITT
findings.headline: Uptake of the council's cost-mitigation schemes remains limited despite available benefits.
findings.detail: The paper identifies that uptake of Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training is limited due to awareness barriers. Many families remain unaware of the full range of support available or how it can be adapted to their circumstances. The council is attempting to address this through improved communications and stakeholder engagement.
findings.matters: If cost management depends on increasing uptake of alternative schemes to offset rising demand, but current uptake is limited and awareness barriers persist, the strategy may not deliver expected savings.
findings.figures: No uptake figures provided
findings.quote: despite these benefits, uptake of Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training was limited due to a number of barriers, and that although existing policies provide flexibility, these options were not widely understood.

findings.headline: The council acknowledges significant cost pressures in school transport driven by increasing demand.
findings.detail: The scrutiny review was triggered by increasing demand for Home to School Transport. The Board recognized significant cost pressures in this area alongside increased demand for SEND support and national reforms. The council is attempting to manage rising costs by increasing uptake of Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training programs, though current uptake remains limited.
findings.matters: A council facing significant acknowledged cost pressures in a major service area where demand is increasing represents a material budget risk and sustainability concern for lenders.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided in this paper
findings.quote: the Board recognised the wider national context of increased demand for both special educational needs and disability (SEND) support and Home to School Transport, significant cost pressures, and national reforms.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation programme paused mid-planning with April 1, 2028 vesting date no longer certain
findings.detail: Government announced on 16 July 2026 a modified unitary authority proposal with 1 April 2028 vesting date. However, the Secretary of State has since announced the LGR programme has been paused for a rapid review. Transition capacity funding allocations are currently being negotiated with government, leaving timing and funding uncertain.
findings.matters: A pause mid-planning of a structural reorganisation with a 16-month vesting date creates uncertainty about transition costs, resource requirements, and execution risk—factors affecting the council's operational stability and medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: Originally scheduled vesting date: 1 April 2028; announcement of pause (date not specified in document)
findings.quote: The Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government has announced that the local government reorganisation programme has been paused while a rapid review is undertaken.

findings.headline: Oracle ERP Phase 3 payroll implementation scheduled for November 2026 with 'little contingency left' after extended testing
findings.detail: Phase 3 of Oracle (HR and Payroll for around 10,000 users) is the most complex and critical element. The second parallel payroll run was extended to meet quality thresholds, leaving minimal contingency in the programme. Live payroll migration is planned for November 2026. The paper acknowledges ongoing concerns around build quality, resourcing, and data migration, noting it is not possible to entirely mitigate against potential issues.
findings.matters: A critical payroll system implementation with extended quality cycles and depleted contingency entering its final phase creates execution risk; payroll failure is a critical service failure affecting 10,000 staff and potentially impairing the council's ability to meet statutory payments.
findings.figures: Phase 3 affects approximately 10,000 users; scheduled live payroll November 2026; contingency described as minimal
findings.quote: the second exercise was extended in order to hit the required quality threshold, leaving little contingency left in the programme.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves projected at only £3.9m by 2030, excluding additional draws required for budget balancing
findings.detail: Total strategic reserves are projected to be £3.9m by 2030, which excludes any additional draws required to balance budgets in 2026/27 or beyond. This represents the council's financial buffer after all planned mitigation, including the £70m EFS.
findings.matters: Reserves of £3.9m provide minimal buffer for a council managing complex statutory services (social care, education, safeguarding) with significant demand volatility—leaving the council vulnerable to unexpected pressures and with limited capacity to manage in-year shortfalls.
findings.figures: £3.9m strategic reserves projected by 2030 (excluding additional draws for 2026/27 and beyond)
findings.quote: Total strategic reserves are projected to be £3.9m by 2030, which excludes any additional draws required to balance budgets in 2026/27 or beyond.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review settlement 11% (below 15% national average) combined with £117.7m cumulative deficit by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 has had significant negative impact on East Sussex funding over three years. The council's Core Spending Power increase is expected to be 11%, below the national average of 15%, even with assumed Council Tax increases of 5% per annum. Despite mitigation actions, the council projects a cumulative deficit of £117.7m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A council receiving below-average funding growth while carrying a cumulative deficit approaching £118m over three years faces a structural squeeze that cannot be resolved through council tax alone—indicating either significant unplanned service reductions or continued reliance on government support.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power increase 11% vs national average 15%; cumulative deficit £117.7m by 2028/29; assumed Council Tax increases 5% per annum
findings.quote: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 has had a significant negative impact on the funding available for East Sussex over the next three years. Our Core Spending Power increase over the settlement period, as indicated by the Provisional Financial Settlement is expected to be 11%, below the national average of 15%.

findings.headline: Council requesting £70m Exceptional Financial Support to cover £55.6m 2026/27 deficit, with repeated need likely for 2027/28
findings.detail: East Sussex has submitted a request for up to £70m of capitalisation to MHCLG to balance the 2026/27 budget. The government has provided agreement in principle. However, EFS is only provided for one financial year and must be paid back. The council has notified MHCLG that without further government funding to address underlying challenges, it is likely to require EFS again for 2027/28 to deliver statutory duties.
findings.matters: A council requiring exceptional financial support to cover its operating deficit, followed by notice of likely repeat demand, signals structural imbalance between statutory obligations and available resources—a fundamental concern for any lender assessing the council's long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £55.6m deficit for 2026/27; £70m capitalisation requested; cumulative deficit of £117.7m by 2028/29
findings.quote: Our revenue budget for 2026/27 includes a £55.6m deficit, which has led us to request Exceptional Financial Support from Government... we have notified MHCLG that without further Government funding to address the challenges we face, we are likely to require EFS for 2027/28 to deliver our statutory duties.

findings.headline: Uptake of both schemes remains limited despite financial benefit and policy flexibility, due to parental concerns, awareness gaps, and practical barriers
findings.detail: The review found that families are often unaware of the flexibility available in Personal Travel Budgets (trial periods, part-week use, flexibility) and of Independent Travel Training itself. Barriers include parental anxiety about safety and independence, concerns about losing existing support if arrangements prove unsuitable, practical difficulties with work schedules and wraparound care, and in rural areas, limited public transport. The council's communications do not adequately address these barriers.
findings.matters: Low uptake of cost-saving schemes means the council is foregoing savings it could realistically achieve; addressing awareness and concerns is within council control and could materially reduce the budget overspend.
findings.figures: 214 of 5,028 pupils on Personal Travel Budget as at Q2 2025 (4.3%); only 10 of 184 families offered enhanced 65p rate have accepted
findings.quote: The Board found that awareness of both Personal Travel Budgets and Independent Travel Training remained limited among families and young people.

findings.headline: SEND home to school transport: 5,028 pupils supported as at Q2 2025; demand increased due to rising EHCP numbers
findings.detail: East Sussex has experienced significant increase in demand for SEND transport over the last three years, mirroring national trends where SEND pupils aged 0-16 account for almost three-quarters of the £2.32bn national spend. The council is responding with route optimisation, solo taxi reduction, and the Personal Travel Budget and Independent Travel Training schemes, but these can only partially offset demand growth.
findings.matters: Demand growth exceeds savings from efficiency measures, creating structural budget pressure; any new funding reform or policy change affecting EHCP or inclusion could materially worsen the position.
findings.figures: 5,028 pupils receiving Home to School Transport support as at end Q2 2025 (out of 67,097 total school pupils); national spending £2.32bn in 2023-24; national 70% increase in real terms 2015/16-2023/24
findings.quote: Mirroring the national trend, the department has seen a significant increase in demand and eligibility for Home to School Transport in the last three years (outlined in the graph below) due to an increase in the number of EHCPs being issued and the number of children eligible for Home to School Transport support.

findings.headline: Independent Travel Training shows cost avoidance of £7,700-£18,100 per pupil annually but uptake is low and a waiting list exists
findings.detail: The programme trains young people to travel independently by public transport, costing average £2,750 per pupil but displacing transport costs of £7,734-£18,112 annually. In 2024-25, 22 pupils were trained with a 96% success rate. The programme has a waiting list of 6 pupils, indicating immediate capacity to expand. Current delivery is focused on pupils aged 16+.
findings.matters: Each trained pupil generates substantial avoided costs (3-7 times the training cost) yet uptake is constrained; expansion could provide significant further savings if barriers to participation can be addressed.
findings.figures: Average ITT cost £2,750 per pupil; average annual transport cost avoided £7,734-£18,112 per child; 22 pupils trained 2024-25 (96% success rate); 6 pupils on waiting list
findings.quote: Independent Travel Training costs an average of £2,750 per pupil. By comparison, the average annual cost of Home to School Transport for pupils attending schools that currently participate in Independent Travel Training ranges from £7,734 to £18,112 per child.

findings.headline: Enhanced Personal Travel Budget offer of 65p per mile (vs standard 45p) has generated £221,000 annual saving in first year
findings.detail: The council introduced an enhanced Personal Travel Budget rate in 2025 to incentivise families to arrange their own transport instead of using higher-cost solo taxi provision. The offer has been made to 184 families, with 10 accepting by Q2 2025. Uptake remains limited but the early savings demonstrate the financial benefit of increased take-up.
findings.matters: Shows management action to redirect spending from high-cost taxis to lower-cost budgets, with early evidence of financial benefit; scaling uptake could materially reduce overspend.
findings.figures: 65p per mile rate; £221,000 estimated annual saving at Q2 2025; offered to 184 families, 10 accepted
findings.quote: The Board heard that ESCC's enhanced offer of 65p per mile for pupils currently using solo transport had generated an estimated £221,000 annual saving as reported at quarter 2 2025.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport budget overran by £3.8m in 2024-25 on a £23m base, driven primarily by demand for SEND provision
findings.detail: The council's spend on home to school transport exceeded budget by 16.5% in 2024-25. The overspend is dominated by transport for pupils with SEND, which has seen a 70% real-terms increase nationally since 2015-16 and is being driven by rising numbers of Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) being issued to pupils in East Sussex.
findings.matters: A significant and growing overspend in a statutory service signals both immediate cash pressure and a structural demand challenge that threatens future financial sustainability unless addressed.
findings.figures: £3.8m overspend on £23m budget; 70% national increase in real terms 2015/16-2023/24; almost three quarters of national increase was SEND aged 0-16
findings.quote: The ESCC budget for Home to School Transport in 2024/25 was £23m and the department overspent by £3.8m; transport for pupils with SEND accounted for the majority of spend.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 5 - Quarter 1 Revenue Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: Authority's reported £0.6m underspend is entirely dependent on unbudgeted grant income and interest income; operational position is £0.6m overspend
findings.detail: The approved budget was balanced at £0 net expenditure. Q1 shows gross expenditure £606k over budget, but the net position is reported as £603k underspend because £1.2m of additional income (£365k additional SDS grant, £341k additional LEVI grant, £150k ASF transition funding, and £353k interest income) was received and included post-budget approval. Without these one-off income sources, the budget position would be significantly negative.
findings.matters: The authority's apparent financial health depends entirely on temporary government grants that may not continue and interest income that will decline with falling rates; the true operational position shows material overspend
findings.figures: Approved budget: £32m, Q1 expenditure forecast: £32.6m overspend, offset by additional income: SDS £365k, LEVI £341k, ASF £150k, Interest £353k
findings.quote: Income is forecast to exceed the approved budget by £1.21 million, reflecting additional Government funding received during the year comprising: additional Spatial Development Strategy (SDS) grant of £0.37 million, additional Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (LEVI) grant of £0.34 million, Adult Skills Fund (ASF) transition funding of £0.15 million; and Forecasted Interest Income of £0.35 million.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 5 - Quarter 1 Revenue Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: Corporate contingency maintained only through reliance on forecasted interest income; underlying budget position is overspend
findings.detail: The Board drew down £300k from the £500k contingency in July to fund fire transition costs. Section 4.2 proposes reinstating this £300k using £353k of forecasted interest income, meaning the contingency buffer now depends on current cash balances and interest rate levels. The base expenditure budget shows a £606k overspend offset entirely by £1.2m of one-off income sources (additional grants and interest).
findings.matters: A contingency restored from temporary interest income is fragile; falling interest rates or cash deployment would eliminate this buffer precisely when a new organization establishing itself needs maximum financial flexibility
findings.figures: Contingency: £500k original, £200k after drawdown, £500k after proposed reinstatement; Interest income forecast: £0.353m
findings.quote: Considering the current forecast outturn and the additional financial capacity provided by the forecast interest income, it is proposed that £300,000 is reinstated to the corporate contingency, restoring the contingency balance to £500,000 and strengthening the Authority's operational resilience.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 5 - Quarter 1 Revenue Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: Permanent recruitment falling behind schedule; interim staffing extended, driving Organisational Operations overspend of £492k
findings.detail: Section 3.2 states the Authority 'has not been possible to recruit the required number of suitably experienced permanent staff or secondees as quickly as originally anticipated' and has extended interim appointments as a result. Organisational Operations forecasts £3.471m against £2.978m budget, a £492k overspend driven by higher interim staffing costs.
findings.matters: Interim staff typically cost more than permanent roles; extended interim appointments in a newly formed organization signal recruitment or affordability challenges, creating cost overruns and organizational continuity risk
findings.figures: Organisational Operations: £2.978m budget vs £3.471m forecast (£492k overspend)
findings.quote: it has not been possible to recruit the required number of suitably experienced permanent staff or secondees as quickly as originally anticipated to support delivery. In response, the Authority has extended the tenure of some existing interim appointments to maintain organisational capacity and business continuity.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 5 - Quarter 1 Revenue Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: Fire and Rescue Services transition to SBSA estimated at £2m across two years, unbudgeted and unfunded by government
findings.detail: The Transition Programme shows £487k expenditure in Q1 with no allocation in the original budget. Section 3.3 discloses that total transition costs are estimated at approximately £2m across 2026/27 and 2027/28. The Authority requested additional government funding but has received none at this stage, leaving the transition costs unfunded.
findings.matters: A substantial unbudgeted cost for a major service transfer planned for April 2027 creates a material financial pressure with no identified funding source, affecting forward budget position and financial resilience
findings.figures: £487k spent in Q1, estimated £2m total transition cost 2026/27-2027/28
findings.quote: The collective cost of delivering all planned transition of services into SBSA is currently estimated at approximately £2 million across 2026/27 and 2027/28. Representations have been made to Government seeking additional financial support towards these costs; however, no additional funding has been offered at this stage.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: MHCLG mandates single Fire & Rescue precept from 2027-28, but the authority and partners have contested this and prefer to maintain two separate precepts
findings.detail: Government has stated the SBSA must set a single precept for Fire & Rescue from 2027-28. However the authority and partner councils have formally raised in consultation their preference to keep two precepts and harmonise them over time instead. Precept levels to be determined in autumn.
findings.matters: A mandated precept arrangement contrary to local preference signals governance tension and could indicate wider local-government funding constraints; implementation complexity may increase if SBSA continues to resist
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: MHCLG have indicated that SBSA will need to set a single precept for Fire & Rescue Services in their area for 2027-28 onwards although the preference of maintaining two precepts which can be harmonised over time has been raised with MHCLG by partners in response to a recent consultation.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision policy for borrowing remains in draft and will be developed in September
findings.detail: MRP policy, which determines how quickly borrowing must be repaid, is described as draft and scheduled for development in September. This is a fundamental component of borrowing strategy and budget affordability.
findings.matters: MRP policy choices directly affect borrowing costs, reserves requirements, and revenue pressure; finalising it after budget principles are approved risks late-stage changes to the financial envelope
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) for borrowing based on draft MRP policy to be developed in September

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Government 'Rewiring the State' policy will reshape local government, but budget is being built with no assumptions about its impact until 28 October
findings.detail: The authority explicitly makes no assumptions about Rewiring the State until the autumn budget on 28 October clarifies the policy. Adjustments will then be made to the MTFP. This creates a lag between budget-setting and policy clarity that could require rework.
findings.matters: Rewiring the State could fundamentally change local government structure, funding, or responsibilities; building a plan with known unknowns creates execution risk
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: No assumptions have been made about the impact of 'Rewiring the State' until further clarity emerges (anticipated with the autumn budget on 28 October). Adjustments will be made to the assumptions following specific policies in the October 28 budget which will impact on the SBSA

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 7 - Bus Reform and Franchising
findings.headline: Bus operators may defer or reduce capital investment while the study explores different future operating models.
findings.detail: The report identifies that study-related uncertainty about the future operating environment could cause operators to defer or cut planned investment in vehicles, depots, facilities, technology and workforce. The council plans to mitigate this through close operator engagement, but the risk is acknowledged and unresolved.
findings.matters: Reduced operator investment could degrade service quality and coverage during and after the study period, affecting resident mobility and potentially economic activity across the area.
findings.figures: 12-month study timeline from commencement
findings.quote: As a result of this uncertainty, some operators may choose to defer or reduce planned investment in vehicles, depots, facilities, technology or workforce development until there is more clarity regarding future arrangements.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 7 - Bus Reform and Franchising
findings.headline: Future implementation of bus reform recommendations is explicitly not covered by this grant approval.
findings.detail: The £564,000 grant fully funds the study itself and a dedicated Bus Officer role. However, the report states that any costs arising from implementing the study's recommendations must be sourced separately. The Authority is not committed to any particular reform outcome, but should the study recommend changes, funding them would be the council's responsibility.
findings.matters: This creates a potential future unfunded liability. Depending on what the study recommends, the council could face material costs for bus system reform with no current budget provision.
findings.figures: £564,000 total (£500,000 study, £64,000 Bus Officer); study duration approximately 12 months
findings.quote: Any costs exceeding the available grant funding, or any financial commitments arising from subsequent implementation of the study's recommendations, are not covered by this approval.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Final financing decision and treasury strategy deferred to December; MRP principles still being developed
findings.detail: The board approved the £3.3m capital commitment but deferred the choice between internal (borrowing against cash reserves) and external borrowing (PWLB) to December's budget meeting. MRP principles—which determine ongoing revenue charges for the capital—will be brought to Audit & Governance Committee in autumn. This means the precise revenue impact remains uncertain until those decisions are made.
findings.matters: Indicates the authority has not yet finalized its treasury strategy for this significant capital commitment; lenders need certainty about financial planning, and the wide 9-15% financing cost range reflects genuine uncertainty about how this will be funded.
findings.figures: 9-15% annual financing cost range (uncertainty indicated), decision deferred to December 2026
findings.quote: Note that approval of Recommendation A (above) will have an impact on the revenue budget for 2027-28 and potentially future years, whichever option is used to finance the capital expenditure, and that final decisions on financing options will be brought for consideration by the Board as part of the development of the 2027-28 revenue budget and 2027-31 Medium Term Financial Plan to the December Board meeting.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Fire appliances reaching end of operational lifecycle with public safety implications; aging fleet drives urgent replacement need
findings.detail: West Sussex Fire & Rescue Services has appliances 'reaching the end of their operational lifecycle' and at risk of 'mechanical failure which could impact negatively on public safety.' The 12 new appliances are operationally essential, not discretionary. This safety imperative is driving the capital decision despite budget constraints, and West Sussex County Council will pay c£1.5m for chassis this year, with SBSA responsible for final c£3.3m payment in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council has essential non-discretionary capital needs that override budget planning; lenders need to assess whether the authority will be forced into unplanned borrowing for critical operational requirements.
findings.figures: 12 fire appliances and 8 4x4 vehicles required, c£1.5m for chassis (WSCC funding), c£3.3m for final payments (SBSA)
findings.quote: West Sussex Fire and Rescue Services has a number of fire appliances and other vehicles which are reaching the end of their operational lifecycle and which, if not replaced in a timely way, will become increasingly at risk of mechanical failure which could impact negatively on public safety.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: New authority commits to £3.3m capital in 2027-28 with no current budget and insufficient uncommitted revenue to cover £300-500k annual financing costs
findings.detail: SBSA has approved capital expenditure for 12 fire appliances from West Sussex Fire & Rescue Service (final costs estimated £3.3m in 2027-28), but no budget allocation exists for this. Financing costs (interest and MRP) will be 9-15% annually, potentially £500k in 2027-28 alone. The paper explicitly states SBSA 'is unlikely to have sufficient uncommitted revenue to cover this cost', creating budget pressure in the authority's second year.
findings.matters: This represents unbudgeted capital spending for a new authority that will force either revenue reallocation or additional borrowing; lenders need to understand whether the council can absorb £300-500k in annual financing costs or whether this signals tighter financial constraints than budgeted.
findings.figures: £3.3m capital, 9-15% annual financing, £500,000 potential revenue cost in 2027-28
findings.quote: There is currently no approved budget within the Strategic Authority for this expenditure next year. It is likely that the cost of financing the proposed capital expenditure of £3.3m could be up to £500,000 of revenue in 2027-28 depending on when the cost was incurred in the year.

findings.headline: Significant under-borrowing position of £112.9m due to strategic decision to delay external borrowing
findings.detail: The council is under-borrowed by £112.919m against its Capital Financing Requirement, having deliberately chosen not to undertake new long-term external borrowing in 2025/26. The Treasury Management Strategy states this was to 'delay borrowing whilst interest rates remain elevated', instead funding the capital programme through internal resources such as useable reserves.
findings.matters: Reliance on internal reserves rather than long-term borrowing to fund capital programmes reduces financial flexibility and suggests the council may face rising borrowing costs or reserve constraints if capital demands continue.
findings.figures: Forecast under-borrowing of £112.919m against CFR of £313.061m; zero new long-term external borrowing despite borrowing requirement of £26.571m
findings.quote: The strategy throughout the year forecast that the level of reserves and balances in the medium term would allow for internal borrowing (using internal resources such as useable reserves or temporary working capital) to support the capital programme. Therefore no new long-term external borrowing was undertaken during 2025/26 in support of the strategic decision to delay borrowing whilst interest rates remain elevated.

findings.headline: Council required short-term borrowing to cover Q4 cashflow shortfalls
findings.detail: The council needed temporary short-term borrowing of £13.8m at 4.75% to cover intra-year liquidity gaps during Q4, sourced from the Local Authority market and an overdraft facility with NatWest. This overdraft was repaid fully in early April 2026.
findings.matters: Reliance on short-term borrowing indicates the council faced Q4 cashflow pressure and was unable to cover temporary shortfalls from reserves or cash generation alone.
findings.figures: £13.8m short-term borrowing at 4.75% average rate; overdraft repaid fully in early April
findings.quote: Short term borrowing was required to cover temporary cashflow shortfalls during Q4. This was sourced from the Local Authority market via the Council's approved brokers or the Council's bank (NatWest) in the form of an authorised overdraft

findings.headline: Cash investment balances fell 74% in one year, from £115.3m to £30.4m
findings.detail: Investment balances have declined dramatically, from £115.3m at Q4 2024/25 to £30.4m at Q4 2025/26. This reflects the council using internal resources and reserves to fund capital programmes rather than borrowing externally, combined with investing cash at shorter durations due to cashflow demands.
findings.matters: A sharp drawdown of investment balances signals the council is depleting liquid reserves, which affects medium-term liquidity and its capacity to absorb shocks without recourse to external borrowing.
findings.figures: Cash investment balances fell from £115.3m to £30.4m (74% reduction); average investment balance declined from £151.972m (Q1) to £51.074m (Q4)
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 31 March 2026 have fallen by 74% in one year, from £115.3m at Q4 2024/25 to £30.4m.

findings.headline: The audit plan identifies a new risk from implementation of Oracle financial systems (excluding Payroll)
findings.detail: Grant Thornton has flagged a new risk relating to the Oracle systems implementation. This is the first year the Council's Statement of Accounts have been prepared using data from the Oracle system, creating implementation risks that could affect control quality and financial reporting accuracy.
findings.matters: System implementation risks can compromise the reliability of financial statements and internal controls, affecting the council's financial governance and potentially masking emerging problems
findings.quote: New risk arising from the implementation of Oracle financial systems (excluding Payroll)

findings.headline: Auditors have identified a significant weakness in the Council's financial sustainability
findings.detail: Interim audit work has flagged a significant weakness in Financial Sustainability as part of the Value for Money assessment. Grant Thornton explicitly note this is unsurprising given the financial challenges the council faces. Additional risk-based procedures will be undertaken to assess the extent of weaknesses, with a separate Annual Value for Money Report to follow.
findings.matters: A significant audit weakness in financial sustainability directly indicates risk to the council's ability to maintain balanced budgets and service delivery, affecting its creditworthiness
findings.quote: Interim work has highlighted a significant weakness with regard to Financial Sustainability. This is no surprise given the financial challenges the Council faces

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: The Revenue MTFP beyond 2026-27 is not considered certain enough for Board approval; formal approval deferred to 2027.
findings.detail: The paper states 'it is not considered that the Revenue MTFP is yet certain enough for future years to seek approval from the Board'. Formal approval for capital and revenue MTFP and budget for 2027-28 is planned for November 2026, then approval in January 2027. This means financial plans for £146m+ budgets are still in development.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender would expect medium-term financial planning to be finalized when major service transitions are imminent. Deferring approval of years 2-4 suggests either funding uncertainty or that organizational priorities remain undefined.
findings.figures: MTFP deferred; approval timeline: November 2026 (draft), January 2027 (final)
findings.quote: As the SBSA is still developing and determining its future priorities and costs and is still receiving more detail regarding future funding flows, it is not considered that the Revenue MTFP is yet certain enough for future years to seek approval from the Board

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Five major service transitions have timing dependent on pending government and constituent council decisions, creating financial planning uncertainty.
findings.detail: Transitions scheduled between March 2027 and May 2028 for Fire & Rescue, Growth Hubs, Adult Skills, Local Transport Authority, and Sussex Police are explicitly described as 'still subject to final decisions from either government or constituent councils'. This uncertainty affects the MTFP's foundation since scope and timing are not confirmed.
findings.matters: Lenders need certainty about what the authority will actually operate and when it assumes responsibility. Undefined transition dates and scope create planning uncertainty and budget volatility.
findings.quote: A number of the forecast transitions and their anticipated timings are still subject to final decisions from either government or constituent councils, but for the purpose of the developing revenue MTFP the key transitions anticipated by the Strategic Authority are as follows (in chronological order).

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Board approving £300k drawdown from contingency for Fire & Rescue transition, reducing contingency from £500k to £200k.
findings.detail: The approved 2026-27 contingency of £500k is being depleted by £300k to fund transition capacity (finance, contracts, HR, legal, project management). This leaves £200k (40% of original) as buffer for 2026-27. The drawdown is positioned as temporary pending government funding recovery, but reduces financial flexibility during a period of major organizational change.
findings.matters: Contingency reserves absorb unexpected costs. Depleting them to 40% of original while managing five major service transitions increases financial vulnerability and signals the authority was inadequately funded for anticipated responsibilities.
findings.figures: £500k total contingency; £300k release proposed; £200k remaining
findings.quote: it is proposed that approval is given by the Board to release £300k from the contingency in the approved budget to secure the required capacity (covering finance, contracts, HR, legal and project/change management) to effect the transition from an SBSA perspective...If approved this would leave £200k remaining in the contingency for 2026-27.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: SBSA has received zero government funding for Fire & Rescue transition despite government allocating £300k to the fire services.
findings.detail: The two fire services have been allocated £100k (East Sussex) and £200k (West Sussex) for their transition costs, totalling £300k. However, SBSA received no government funding. The paper notes these allocations are 'likely not to cover the additional costs of transition' and present 'a risk to adequately resourcing an operationally effective transfer', with discussions ongoing with MHCLG to address this gap.
findings.matters: A funding mismatch between service providers and the receiving authority creates operational and financial risk. The authority is responsible for managing the transition but must fund it from its own resources.
findings.figures: £100k (East Sussex Fire & Rescue), £200k (West Sussex County Council), £0 for SBSA
findings.quote: However, the SBSA has so far not been allocated any funds to support its costs regarding transition of Fire & Rescue Services, and discussions are taking place with officials in MHCLG regarding this lack of funding support.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Revenue budget forecast to expand from £32.5m to £185.6m by 2029-30 through five major service transitions, but operational capacity remains uncertain.
findings.detail: The MTFP shows 2027-28 at £146.278m and 2028-29 at £183.527m, driven by Fire & Rescue (by March 2027), Growth Hubs (Spring 2027), Adult Skills (Sept 2027), Local Transport Authority (May 2028), and Sussex Police (May 2028). The paper states this step change will require additional capacity beyond what is currently budgeted, with 'further capacity likely required in both 2026-27 and 2027-28' but the quantum is undefined.
findings.matters: Lenders assess an authority's ability to manage major organizational change. A six-fold budget expansion without finalized staffing plans or confirmed funding for all transitions creates execution risk.
findings.quote: The MTFP shows that the 2027-28 revenue budget is likely to be around £146m, rising to around £185m by 2028-29, an increase of six times that of the comparable revenue budget in 2026 -27. To ensure this step change in programming is effectively delivered we will require additional capacity in the Sussex & Brighton Strategic Authority (SBSA).

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £36.4m above forecast to £313.061m, indicating capital programme expansion
findings.detail: The closing Capital Financing Requirement (underlying borrowing need for capital spending) was £313.061m against an original estimate of £276.672m, a variance of £36.389m. The paper does not explain whether this is due to overspending on existing projects, acceleration of schemes, or new capital added to the programme. Despite this larger capital need, no new external borrowing was undertaken.
findings.matters: Capital programme growth beyond forecast, combined with financing from depleting reserves rather than sustainable external borrowing, raises questions about affordability and the sustainability of future capital spending.
findings.figures: Closing CFR £313.061m actual vs £276.672m forecast; £36.389m variance
findings.quote: The closing CFR showed an under-borrowing position of £112.919m, compared to the original estimate of £70.000m under-borrowed.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing of £13.8m required in Q4 to cover temporary cashflow shortfalls, indicating working capital pressure
findings.detail: The council borrowed £13.8m on a short-term basis (overdraft from NatWest and Local Authority market) during Q4 to manage temporary cashflow timing mismatches, though this was repaid in full by early April 2026. The need for short-term borrowing even in a single quarter suggests underlying working capital pressure.
findings.matters: Reliance on short-term borrowing to cover routine quarter-end cashflow gaps indicates potential misalignment between spending patterns and cash receipts, which can constrain operations or incur unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £13.8m short-term borrowing at 31 March 2026 (repaid April 2026); 4.75% average rate
findings.quote: Short term borrowing was required to cover temporary cashflow shortfalls during Q4. This was sourced from the Local Authority market via the Council's approved brokers or the Council's bank (NatWest) in the form of an authorised overdraft; the overdraft as at 31 March 2026 was repaid fully in early April.

findings.headline: Under-borrowing increased to £112.919m as capital spending was funded from internal resources, not external debt
findings.detail: The council's closing under-borrowing position (capital need vs external borrowing) was £112.919m, significantly higher than the £70.000m originally forecast. This occurred because no new long-term external borrowing was undertaken in 2025/26; instead, capital expenditure was funded from useable reserves and temporary working capital. The paper states borrowing will be 'considered in the context of the wider treasury management position and economic environment during 2026/27', implying borrowing may become necessary as rates normalise.
findings.matters: This shows the council is consciously deferring borrowing and relying on depleting internal reserves to fund capital, a strategy that depends on adequate reserve levels and eventual access to external debt at acceptable rates.
findings.figures: £112.919m under-borrowing at outturn vs £70.000m estimate; £0m new long-term borrowing undertaken
findings.quote: Therefore no new long-term external borrowing was undertaken during 2025/26 in support of the strategic decision to delay borrowing whilst interest rates remain elevated.

findings.headline: Investment cash balances have fallen by 74% in one year, from £115.3m to £30.4m, depleting liquid reserves
findings.detail: The council's cash investment balances fell dramatically from £115.3m at Q4 2024/25 to £30.4m at Q4 2025/26. The paper attributes this to a strategic decision to use internal resources—useable reserves and temporary working capital—to fund the capital programme rather than take new external borrowing whilst interest rates remain elevated. While the investment performance is strong (4.19% return vs 3.73% benchmark), the absolute liquidity position is now substantially lower.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on cash reserves and liquidity, as a 74% depletion in one year significantly reduces financial headroom and flexibility to manage pressures or unexpected demands.
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 31 March 2026 have fallen by 74% in one year, from £115.3m at Q4 2024/25 to £30.4m.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation announcement delayed, deferring £50k in anticipated actuarial advisory work
findings.detail: Government's announcement of LGR plans for Sussex was deferred from April 2026 due to ongoing consultation on unitary authority structure. East Sussex had budgeted £50k for actuarial advice if employers in the fund faced merger or disaggregation, but this work is now pending LGR outcomes.
findings.matters: LGR could materially restructure the council and affect pension fund employer membership and liabilities; planning uncertainty persists until government confirms shape of new authorities
findings.figures: £50k reduction in Actuary Fund work line
findings.quote: Government were due to announce the plans for Sussex in April 2026, however this has now been delayed due to the consultation taking place on the shape of the Sussex unitary authorities continues.

findings.headline: Payroll System Enhancement and Helpdesk projects deferred to 2026/27, deferring £92k in planned IT investment
findings.detail: The Payroll System Enhancement is on hold pending completion of the Guaranteed Minimum Pension (GMP) project (now expected June 2026). The Helpdesk project was delayed by IT resource constraints. These deferrals created underspends of £71k in IT costs and £21k in admin support but create carry-forward obligations for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Deferred system implementations affect operational efficiency; GMP project completion is now a critical dependency for payroll system work
findings.figures: IT systems £71k underspend, admin support £21k underspend
findings.quote: These include the Payroll System Enhancement project which was placed on hold until the Guaranteed Minimum Pension (GMP) project is completed (now expected June 2026).

findings.headline: Pension fund administration spending exceeded budget by £147,000 in 2025/26
findings.detail: The fund outturn was £4.792m against the approved budget of £4.645m. While the quarter 4 forecast was revised down by £243k, the actual outturn still came in £147k over budget. The overspend spans multiple line items including staff costs, investment advice, and administration.
findings.matters: Any material budget variance requires explanation and funding adjustments; cumulative overspends can impact reserves and next-year planning
findings.figures: Budget £4.645m, outturn £4.792m, variance £0.147m
findings.quote: The actual outturn of 2025/26 is £4.792m, a decrease of £0.243m from the last projected position but an increase of £0.147m from the approved budget.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: MRP methodology change will increase revenue charges for future debt repayment
findings.detail: The council is changing its Minimum Revenue Provision policy to use the council's prevailing average borrowing rate (currently 4.38%) instead of a flat 2% for annuity calculations on historical expenditure. This increases the annual revenue charge needed to repay debt, reducing available resources for service delivery.
findings.matters: Reduces cash available for other services; reflects higher actual borrowing costs; signals more prudent accounting but tighter financial position
findings.figures: Council average borrowing rate 4.38% vs prior flat 2% assumption
findings.quote: Clarity to the interest rate used for annuity calculations. It is recommended that annuity calculations use an interest rate based on the Council's average rate of all long-term external borrowing. This is a change from the previous methodology, which used a straight 2% interest rate on all charges, regardless of timing of expenditure and asset life.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Investment counterparty limits significantly reduced, indicating liquidity pressure
findings.detail: The council has cut maximum investment limits with individual counterparties to manage risk from its shrinking cash balances. Local authority lending reduced from £60m to £20m per authority; bank lending capped at £20m instead of £60m. These defensive moves signal the council is rationing cash availability.
findings.matters: Suggests acute pressure on liquidity; council is restricting exposure to individual institutions as cash buffer shrinks
findings.figures: Investment portfolio forecast: £73.8m (Nov 2025) declining to £50m (31 March 2026); counterparty limits halved or reduced from prior year
findings.quote: Maximum investment limits on counterparty types been reduced compared to the 2025/26 strategy to avoid over exposure to individual sectors due to reducing investment balances and subsequent risk to overexposure. Limits for investments in individual UK Local Authorities have been reduced from a maximum £60m to £20m per authority.
