findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: By 2028/29 the council may need to borrow for day-to-day revenue expenditure, not just capital
findings.detail: The liability benchmark analysis shows that the Net Loans Requirement is projected to exceed the Loans CFR in 2028/29. This signals that if current financial trends continue, the council will need to borrow not only for capital projects but also to finance routine revenue spending—a significant deterioration in financial position.
findings.matters: Indicates a structural revenue deficit; demonstrates financial trajectory is unsustainable without intervention
findings.figures: Net Loans Requirement projected to exceed Loans CFR from 2028/29 onwards; external borrowing requirement forecast to peak at £647m in 2034/35
findings.quote: The graph shows that the Net Loans Requirement will become greater than the Loans CRF value in 2028/29, suggesting that if the council's financial position continues as expenditure currently forecast, then the Council will need to borrow to finance its day-to-day expenditure in addition to its capital programme and applied capitalisation direction.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Council will shift from internal to external borrowing due to reducing reserves
findings.detail: The council has operated with internal borrowing since 2019/20 using reserves to fund capital needs. However, it now states: 'due to an increasing borrowing requirement, reducing reserves, and the recommendation to apply for Exceptional Financial support...it is likely that the council will need to enter into new borrowing at some point during 2026/27.'
findings.matters: Signals reserves are becoming depleted; external borrowing will carry higher costs than the internal borrowing strategy
findings.figures: External debt £200m; total CFR £313m projected to £404m by 2026/27; under-borrowing position of £113m rising to £209m
findings.quote: The borrowing strategy for 2026/27 will initially focus on meeting this borrowing need from internal borrowing; however, due to an increasing borrowing requirement, reducing reserves, and the recommendation to apply for Exceptional Financial support in the form of capitalisation direction, it is likely that the council will need to enter into new borrowing at some point during 2026/27.

findings.committee: Sussex and Brighton Strategic Authority Board
findings.headline: Council has applied for £70m Exceptional Finance Support to treat revenue costs as capital expenditure
findings.detail: Due to the council's challenging financial position, it has applied to government for a capitalisation direction to allow up to £70m of revenue expenditure to be funded by borrowing or capital receipts rather than from revenue budget in 2026/27. This would significantly alter the council's borrowing profile for that year. Approval from government is required and not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: Government support is necessary to balance the budget; if denied, the council faces a structural funding gap; approval status is uncertain
findings.figures: £70m capitalisation direction borrowing in 2026/27 only; total borrowing requirement rises to £100m in 2026/27 (compared to £29m in prior year)
findings.quote: As set out in the RPPR Budget report to Cabinet on 27 January 2026, due to the Council's overall challenging financial position, the Council has applied to government for Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) for 2026/27 in the form of a capitalisation direction.

findings.headline: Investment balances depleted 58% in one year; council funding capital programme through reserve drawdown
findings.detail: Cash investment balances have fallen from £114.2m at Q3 2024/25 to £57.1m at Q3 2025/26. The council's strategy forecasts using £75.000m of internal resources (reserves and working capital) to finance the capital programme in 2025/26, supplemented by new borrowing of £38.110m, indicating significant dependence on drawing down accumulated reserves.
findings.matters: Substantial depletion of financial reserves reduces the council's buffer against unexpected shocks and financial flexibility; combined with increased capital borrowing, it signals dependence on sustained access to capital markets.
findings.figures: Investment balances down 58% from £114.2m to £57.1m; council planning to use £75.000m internal resources plus £38.110m new borrowing
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 31 December 2025 have fallen by 58% in one year, from £114.2m at Q3 2024/25 to £57.1m.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement revised up to £113.110m, exceeding original forecast by £43.110m (61%)
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement closing position has been revised to £313.252m from the original estimate of £276.672m. The forecast new borrowing requirement increased from £70.000m to £113.110m, reflecting a significantly larger capital programme carried forward from 2024/25 than anticipated when the Treasury Management Strategy was approved in February 2025.
findings.matters: A material upward revision in capital borrowing indicates either programme acceleration or cost escalation; lenders must assess whether the council can afford this additional debt burden and maintain financial sustainability.
findings.figures: New borrowing forecast £113.110m vs original estimate £70.000m; CFR closing position £313.252m vs original estimate £276.672m
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to give rise to new borrowing required of £113.110m by the end of the year, compared to the original estimate of £70.000m following an increased capital programme borrowing need in 2024/25 carried forward.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing of £15m borrowed in December to cover temporary cashflow shortfall
findings.detail: The Council required short-term Local Authority borrowing of £15m in late December 2025 to manage a temporary cashflow gap. The borrowing was scheduled for early January repayment, suggesting a timing issue between expenditure and income within the financial year.
findings.matters: Requirement for short-term emergency borrowing indicates tight cashflow management and potential timing pressures in the Council's cash position during peak spending periods.
findings.figures: £15.000m short-term borrowing at 4.40% average rate
findings.quote: Short term borrowing was required to cover a temporary cashflow shortfall towards the end of December. This was sourced from the Local Authority Market via the Council's approved brokers; the loans will be repaid in early January.

findings.headline: Cash investment balances fell 58% in one year, from £114.2m to £57.1m
findings.detail: The Council's liquid investment holdings declined substantially over twelve months. This reflects the Council drawing down working capital and reserves to fund capital expenditure through internal borrowing, rather than relying solely on external borrowing. The Council is deploying its cash to self-fund capital spending.
findings.matters: A 58% reduction in liquid investments represents a significant drawdown of the Council's financial cushion and its capacity to weather unexpected pressures without raising external borrowing.
findings.quote: Cash investment balances as at 31 December 2025 have fallen by 58% in one year, from £114.2m at Q3 2024/25 to £57.1m.

findings.headline: Borrowing need increased 61% from strategy forecast due to higher capital programme carried forward
findings.detail: The Council's original Treasury Management Strategy (February 2025) forecast new borrowing of £70m would be required in 2025/26. The Q3 forecast now shows borrowing requirement of £113.110m, driven by increased capital programme borrowing needs carried forward from 2024/25. External borrowing requirement remains manageable at £38.110m after accounting for £75m of internal borrowing.
findings.matters: This represents a 61% increase in the borrowing need from the strategy approved just eleven months earlier, indicating material changes to the capital programme that lenders need to monitor.
findings.figures: Original borrowing estimate £70.000m vs revised £113.110m; expected external borrowing £38.110m
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to give rise to new borrowing required of £113.110m by the end of the year, compared to the original estimate of £70.000m following an increased capital programme borrowing need in 2024/25 carried forward.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Audit Report - 13 February 2026
findings.headline: Council unable to back up asset records for property areas; issue persists from prior audit
findings.detail: The council continues to struggle to obtain supporting documentation for gross internal areas (GIA) and land area records—an issue first raised in 2023/24. They are undertaking an ongoing project to remeasure GIAs but the problem has not been resolved.
findings.matters: Inability to properly document and back up property records suggests weak asset management systems, which affects capital asset valuation, security of collateral, and confidence in the council's property data.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: There were instances identified where the Council was unable or struggled to obtain backing for their gross internal areas (GIA) and Land Areas. This issue still persists, having raised in 2023/24, with the Council stating there is an ongoing project to remeasure GIAs.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Audit Report - 13 February 2026
findings.headline: No formal periodic access reviews exist for users authorised to post financial journals
findings.detail: The audit identified that a large number of council staff have ability to post journals but there is no formal process for periodic access reviews to remove or amend rights. The council has addressed this through Oracle system migration with more restricted access.
findings.matters: Lack of formal access controls creates risk of unauthorized or erroneous journal entries in the general ledger, affecting financial record integrity and audit quality.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: In reviewing journal entry controls, it was noted that a large number of users have the ability to post journals. While understanding that the size of the Council team requires that a large number of people have access, and the overall role assignment controls appear appropriate given the size of the Council, we identified that there is no formal process for periodic access reviews to remove or amend rights.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Audit Report - 13 February 2026
findings.headline: PFI schools liability was overstated by £1.7m under the council's calculation method
findings.detail: The council calculated its schools PFI liability using a high-level indexation approach that overstated it by £1.7m compared to a detailed IFRS16 recalculation. Although above trivial materiality, the error remains unadjusted. The council will implement detailed PFI model calculations from 2025/26 onwards to ensure accuracy.
findings.matters: A £1.7m overstatement shows the accounting method was not accurately capturing PFI obligations, which directly affects liability position and debt capacity assessment for lending decisions.
findings.quote: The schools PFI liability has been calculated using a high-level indexation approach. This has overstated the liability compared to the detailed IFRS16 recalculation used by Grant Thornton. At £1.7m the variation, whilst above trivial, has been reported as an unadjusted error.

findings.headline: Policy team staffing reduction will impact Unitary Authority transition support and scrutiny preparation
findings.detail: The council proposes £20k savings through policy team reductions. This 'would have a potential impact on supporting the transition to the new Unitary Authority including preparing the induction of new Members (particularly in relation to RPPR and scrutiny), support for scrutiny engagement in the transition, and support for budget setting processes.'
findings.matters: Reduced governance capacity at the point of major organizational transformation (Unitary Authority transition) could create delivery or control risk
findings.figures: £20k saving
findings.quote: This would have a potential impact on supporting the transition to the new Unitary Authority including preparing the induction of new Members (particularly in relation to RPPR and scrutiny), support for scrutiny engagement in the transition, and support for budget setting processes.

findings.headline: Integrated Night Service contract withdrawal may create greater impact on NHS than on council services
findings.detail: A contract for integrated night service ends 31/08/2026. The council notes that 'the impact of withdrawing funding would be minimal for ESCC but greater for the NHS', indicating the NHS may absorb these costs or reduce service.
findings.matters: This creates relationship risk with NHS partners and potential pressure for future service commitments or emergency funding if the NHS cannot absorb the impact
findings.figures: £276k contract value
findings.quote: Current contract ends 31/08/2026. The impact of withdrawing funding would be minimal for ESCC but greater for the NHS.

findings.headline: Joint Use Agreements review outcome is unknown and dependent on future arrangements
findings.detail: The council proposes £100k savings from reviewing joint use agreements across 2026-27 and 2027-28. However, the likely impact is listed as 'Currently unknown - is dependent on the arrangements put in place.'
findings.matters: £100k in proposed savings with uncertain delivery is a red flag for savings realization risk
findings.figures: £100k annually
findings.quote: Currently unknown - is dependent on the arrangements put in place

findings.headline: New care leavers from 2026/27 will receive loans and bursaries instead of full accommodation funding, saving £50k (£18k 2026/27, £24k 2027/28, £8k 2028/29)
findings.detail: New care leavers from 2026-27 onwards will receive loans and bursaries instead of full accommodation funding. The council notes 'there is a potential impact on number of care leavers who will apply, attend and complete university courses.'
findings.matters: Reducing support for vulnerable young people may increase future demand for adult social care, housing, or benefits, creating secondary financial pressures
findings.quote: There is a potential impact on number of care leavers who will apply, attend and complete university courses, although the rebased offer is in line with a range of other Local Authorities who have similar levels of care leavers attending university.

findings.headline: Climate change activities reduction will inhibit delivery of the Climate Change Action Plan
findings.detail: The Environment division proposes £75k savings through a review of climate change activities. The council explicitly states this 'will inhibit the County Council's ability to deliver the objectives of the Climate Change Action Plan.'
findings.matters: The council is accepting a known constraint on its strategic objectives, which could create reputational, regulatory, or legal risk
findings.figures: £75k saving
findings.quote: Will inhibit the County Council's ability to deliver the objectives of the Climate Change Action Plan.

findings.headline: Business Services must retain capacity to deliver council-wide savings, limiting its own savings realization
findings.detail: The Business Services Department proposes £725k savings but explicitly notes it must retain capacity in the short term to support the broader savings programme. It cannot undertake staff consultations without HR or asset changes without Property support.
findings.matters: Delivery capacity constraints may delay or reduce full realization of the £8m savings programme
findings.figures: £725k proposed reduction on £26,105k net budget
findings.quote: In the short term It is necessary for BSD to retain the capacity to support the delivery of wider savings. For example, it is not possible to undertake robust staff consultations without Human Resources (HR) support or to make changes to the uses of certain assets without Property support.

findings.headline: Future data and insight work will require use of reserves if the council removes consultancy budget
findings.detail: The council proposes removing the £20k annual consultancy budget from Performance, Research and Intelligence. The council explicitly states this means 'any future work required will not be possible without use of reserves.'
findings.matters: This is a direct admission that the council will need to draw on reserves for specific work, which directly affects reserve forecasting and headroom
findings.figures: £20k annual saving
findings.quote: Removal of this budget will mean that any future work required will not be possible without use of reserves.

findings.headline: Council proposes £50k annual savings from increased developer contribution income in 2026/27 and 2027/28, dependent on market conditions
findings.detail: The council proposes £50k annual savings in 2026-27 and 2027-28 from increased developer contribution income. The document explicitly warns that if there is 'an unexpected downturn in the market and/or local matters that stall the delivery of development', this will prevent achievement of these savings.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's savings plan is resilient to economic downturns; development income is cyclical and could force mid-year reprioritization
findings.quote: Income particularly dependent upon market conditions.  Should there be an unexpected downturn in the market and/or local matters that stall the delivery of development, then this will impact upon the ability to achieve this additional income.

findings.headline: Budget deficits forecast across entire MTFP with further exceptional support anticipated for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £55.6m deficit in 2026/27 (dependent on EFS), £80.7m in 2027/28, and £36.9m in 2028/29. The paper states it is 'anticipated that further EFS will be required in 2027/28'. Local government reorganisation expected in 2028/29 is not anticipated to resolve the underlying financial issues. This represents £111m cumulative structural deficit over three years.
findings.matters: Deficits are structural and persistent. Reliance on capitalisation directions is described as 'unsustainable' yet appears necessary annually. Each year of EFS adds financing costs (£6.6m annually for a £70m direction), compounding future pressures and locking in debt service obligations.
findings.figures: £55.6m deficit 2026/27; £80.7m 2027/28; £36.9m 2028/29; £111.1m cumulative; £6.6m annual financing cost per £70m borrowed; further EFS anticipated in 2027/28
findings.quote: Reliance on this mechanism in future years will increase the Council's borrowing requirement and result in higher debt financing costs over the MTFP period.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand accelerating: assessments up 22% versus pre-pandemic despite budget constraints
findings.detail: Care assessments increased 6.9% year-on-year and 22.2% compared to pre-pandemic (2019). Safeguarding inquiries completed are up 80.6% versus 2019. Long-term support caseload up 11.5% compared to November 2019. These trends drive budget investment of £18.9m in 2026/27, but the council states it cannot invest to the level it would want due to funding gap.
findings.matters: Demand is growing faster than resources. Adult social care and children's services budgets have grown 40% and 54% respectively since 2022/23, yet the council reports 'very limited opportunity to make further savings'. This mismatch is structural and will force service rationing or continued reliance on exceptional support.
findings.figures: 6.9% increase assessments YoY; 22.2% increase vs pre-Covid; 80.6% increase safeguarding inquiries vs 2019; 11.5% increase in long-term support caseload; ASC budget up 40% and Children's Services up 54% in 2022/23-2025/26 period
findings.quote: There has been a 6.9% increase in assessments (Care Act, Carers, Continuing Health Care, Occupational Therapy and Sensory) completed between January and November 2025 compared to the same period in 2024, and a 22.2% increase compared to the same period in 2019 (pre-Covid).

findings.headline: SEND deficit of £20.1m will become £76.5m liability when statutory override ends April 2028
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant SEND deficit is currently hidden from the council's accounts by a statutory override. When the override expires in April 2028, the council must recognise the full £76.5m accumulated deficit on its balance sheet. No government funding has been announced to cover this, and the council states it will have 'serious implications for the Council's financial position and borrowing requirement'.
findings.matters: This is a known future liability with a fixed date. In 18 months, the council's reported financial position will materially deteriorate by £76.5m, worsening an already fragile reserves position during the MTFP period when other deficits are also forecast.
findings.figures: £20.1m SEND deficit forecast at 1 April 2026; £76.5m at 1 April 2028 when override expires; national SEND deficit estimated at £14bn by 2027/28, currently expected to be addressed by local government
findings.quote: The SEND deficit is forecast to be £20.1m on 1 April 2026, rising to £76.5m by 1 April 2028, when the statutory override is due to end. At that point, the Council will be required to recognise the full deficit on its balance sheet.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves depleted 68% from £16.5m to forecast £5.2m by 2030, eliminating financial flexibility
findings.detail: Total strategic reserves of £16.5m at April 2025 will fall to £10.5m by April 2026 and £5.2m by April 2030. The Chief Finance Officer states remaining reserves are 'at the absolute minimum level required to safeguard the Council against unforeseen risks and volatility' and warns that further draws would 'leave the Council exposed to an unacceptable level of financial risk'. The council cannot use reserves to bridge the 2026/27 budget gap.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves mean zero buffer for service demand shocks, inflation surprises, or unforeseen costs. Council is operationally vulnerable and dependent on government bailout. This is material to credit rating and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £16.5m → £10.5m → £5.2m; General Fund balance £10.0m; revenue contingency £6.7m (1% of net revenue expenditure); total reserves of £60.1m at April 2026 compared to £88.6m at April 2025
findings.quote: the CFO considers the remaining reserves to be at the absolute minimum level required to safeguard the Council against unforeseen risks and volatility. Any further draw on reserves to support the planned revenue budget would compromise the adequacy of reserves and leave the Council exposed to an unacceptable level of financial risk.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 creates structural £12.6m funding loss over three years with no policy fix available
findings.detail: Changes to the government funding formula reduce East Sussex's settlement funding by £12.6m over the three-year period. Non-Council Tax Core Spending Power will decline 5.8% by 2028/29. The council states this is cash neutral nominally but represents a real-terms reduction of 3-4% when inflation is accounted for. The funding loss is driven by formula changes that fail to account for the council's high social care demand and dispersed rural population.
findings.matters: This is not a demand management or efficiency problem the council can fix; it reflects a deliberate national reallocation of funding away from their area despite high need. Shows structural gap between resources and statutory obligations that will persist across the MTFP.
findings.figures: £12.6m loss over settlement period; 5.8% reduction in non-CT CSP by 2028/29; £17m loss compared to previous funding formula over 3 years; only £21.2m of £71.7m budget growth funded
findings.quote: These changes fail to capture the true cost pressures in delivering statutory services in a county with high social care demand and a dispersed population, with limited opportunities to raise income locally.

findings.headline: Council seeking £70m capitalisation direction to borrow for revenue budget, first time in its history
findings.detail: East Sussex is requesting permission from Government to borrow £70m under Exceptional Financial Support to balance its 2026/27 revenue budget. This is the first time the council has needed to borrow for day-to-day operations rather than capital investment. The budget is contingent on this approval; without it, the Chief Finance Officer would be required to issue a Section 114 report signalling financial distress.
findings.matters: Revenue borrowing indicates structural financial distress. A council with established sound financial management resorting to this measures signals either exceptional external pressures or deteriorating underlying position — both material credit concerns for lenders.
findings.figures: £70m capitalisation direction requested; £55.6m underlying deficit in 2026/27; estimated annual financing cost of £6.6m (£2.9m Minimum Revenue Provision + £3.7m interest) if full £70m borrowed
findings.quote: For the first time, we are not able to present a balanced budget drawing on our own resources and the proposed revenue budget for 2026/27 presented in this report is contingent on Government's agreement to additional support in the form of exceptional permission to borrow to fund day to day services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: Significant unquantifiable risks from Local Government Reorganisation and multiple national policy uncertainties
findings.detail: The CFO identifies several areas of significant unquantifiable change that will impact the financial position: LGR implementation (with no additional funding identified for upfront costs), SEND reform, social care funding changes, Adult Social Care fair pay agreement, environmental targets and climate emergency, plus geopolitical uncertainty on trade and inflation.
findings.matters: Multiple concurrent reforms with no funding create second-order risks. The council cannot quantify these but must hold reserves to cover them—yet reserves are already depleted.
findings.figures: LGR reserve transfer of £4.2m in 2025/26; climate and environment commitments unquantified
findings.quote: Work will continue to identify risks and pressures. In addition, the effects of several national funding decisions will impact on the financial position, the timing of which is yet to be determined. These are significant areas of change that currently are not fully understood and cannot be fully quantified but will have potential significant financial impact

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: Budget is 'not robust nor sustainable in the medium term' and depends on exceptional measures that cannot be repeated indefinitely
findings.detail: The CFO concludes that whilst the 2026/27 budget is legally balanced, 'it is neither robust nor sustainable in the medium term. It depends on exceptional measures that cannot be repeated indefinitely.' The council is borrowing to fund revenue costs (via capitalisation directive), which 'fundamentally undermines long-term sustainability. Borrowing for revenue does not address the structural gap between recurring income and expenditure, meaning the underlying deficit persists.'
findings.matters: The CFO's own assessment that the budget is not sustainable is a stark signal. This is not routine financial stress management but a confession of structural insolvency.
findings.figures: £55.6m deficit in 2026/27; reliance on capitalisation borrowing; savings already delivered of £156m since 2010
findings.quote: while the proposed budget for 2026/27 is legally balanced, it is neither robust nor sustainable in the medium term. It depends on exceptional measures that cannot be repeated indefinitely.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: General Fund Balance of only 1.86% of net revenue expenditure is lowest among all county councils
findings.detail: The CIPFA Resilience Index shows East Sussex holds the lowest unallocated reserve (General Fund) as a percentage of net revenue expenditure at 1.86%, with the next lowest at 2.43% and the highest at 14.39%. The council holds only £10m in general fund balance against a net revenue budget of £693m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Holding the lowest reserves ratio among peers means the council has minimal flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures or demand shocks.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance 1.86% of NRE (lowest among 21 counties); £10m absolute balance; combined with contingency 2.41% of NRE
findings.quote: East Sussex is the lowest at 1.86%, the next lowest being 2.43% and the highest being 14.39%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: SEND deficit growing rapidly; will reach £76.5m by March 2028 when statutory accounting override expires
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs deficit is currently £20.1m as of 1 April 2026 and is forecast to rise to £76.5m by 31 March 2028. When the statutory override ends, this deficit must be recognised on the balance sheet and funded. The CFO notes: 'if the statutory override were not in place during 2026/27, the council would have to increase any EFS request accordingly.'
findings.matters: A £76.5m future liability that suddenly moves onto the balance sheet represents a material risk to the council's financial position and borrowing capacity. No permanent solution has been announced.
findings.figures: SEND deficit £20.1m (1 Apr 2026), rising to £76.5m (31 Mar 2028); no HNB allocation increase for 2026/27
findings.quote: The SEND deficit is forecast to be £20.1m on 1 April 2026, rising to £76.5m by 31 March 2028, when the statutory override is due to end. At that point, the Council will be required to recognise the full deficit on its balance sheet.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 settlement is unfavourable; grant funding reduced by £12.6m over settlement period
findings.detail: The provisional Local Government Finance Settlement of 17 December 2025 confirmed that FFR2.0 changes have significantly reduced the council's Fair Funding Assessment by £12.6m. Non-Council Tax Core Spending Power will reduce by 5.8% by 2028/29. The change from 2025/26 to 2026/27 is cash neutral but 'with inflation currently between 3% to 4%, represents a significant reduction in real terms.'
findings.matters: Falling government funding combined with high inflation means the council faces rising pressure even without demand changes. Counties and rural councils were particularly disadvantaged.
findings.figures: FFA reduction £12.6m over settlement period; non-Council Tax Core Spending Power down 5.8% by 2028/29; inflation 3-4%
findings.quote: the changes to formulae have significantly reduced the Council's share of settlement funding, now known as the Fair Funding Assessment (FFA), which will reduce by £12.6m over the settlement period

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: Cumulative budget deficit projected to reach £111.1m by 2028/29, far exceeding available reserves
findings.detail: Even with all planned savings and spending controls, the Medium Term Financial Plan shows deficits of £55.6m (2026/27), £18.5m (2027/28), and £36.9m (2028/29). The CFO notes this 'would significantly exceed the level of reserves available to balance the budget' and that 'local action alone cannot restore sustainability.'
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit that cannot be closed through savings or reserves means the council cannot be financially sustainable without fundamental reform or additional government support.
findings.quote: Total service and strategic reserves are projected to reduce to £16.1m by 2030. As a result of ongoing demand and inflationary pressures, and a lack of additional government funding, the cumulative deficit is projected to grow to £111.1m by 2028/29, which would significantly exceed the level of reserves available to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: Strategic reserves exhausted to absolute minimum; no further draws can be recommended
findings.detail: The council has drawn £25.7m from reserves over two years (£14.3m in 2024/25, £11.4m in 2025/26). The CFO states remaining reserves are now at absolute minimum and 'Any further draw on reserves to support the revenue budget would compromise my statutory responsibility as set out in 1.2 of this statement and leave the Council exposed to an unacceptable level of financial risk. Consequently, no additional use of reserves can be recommended to bridge the budget gap for 2026/27.'
findings.matters: Reserves are the only buffer against unexpected demand or costs. A council with no capacity to draw reserves for emergencies signals extreme financial stress.
findings.figures: Strategic reserves: £16.5m (Apr 2025) → £10.5m (Apr 2026) → £5.2m (Apr 2030); Total reserves projected to £46m by 2030
findings.quote: Any further draw on reserves to support the revenue budget would compromise my statutory responsibility as set out in 1.2 of this statement and leave the Council exposed to an unacceptable level of financial risk. Consequently, no additional use of reserves can be recommended to bridge the budget gap for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Reserves and Robustness Statement Cabinet 27.01.26
findings.headline: Council depends entirely on Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG or will have to issue a Section 114 notice
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumes MHCLG will grant EFS to allow the council to borrow to fund revenue expenditure via a capitalisation directive. The CFO explicitly states: 'If MHCLG do not grant the capitalisation request the Council will not be able to balance the 2026/27 budget and I will have no option but to use my statutory powers and issue a section 114 notice in the absence of further measures.'
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a statutory warning of insolvency and triggers external intervention. For a lender, this is the most severe signal of financial distress.
findings.figures: £55.6m financial gap for 2026/27
findings.quote: If MHCLG do not grant the capitalisation request the Council will not be able to balance the 2026/27 budget and I will have no option but to use my statutory powers and issue a section 114 notice in the absence of further measures.

findings.headline: Forecast investment returns for 2026/27 are 3.59%, down from 5.26% in 2024/25 and 4.63% in H1 2025/26
findings.detail: Forecast investment returns for 2026/27 are 3.59%, down from 5.26% in 2024/25 and 4.63% in H1 2025/26. This reduces the income available to offset borrowing costs precisely when the Council is moving into external borrowing.
findings.matters: Falling investment returns remove a source of revenue that could cushion budget pressures and intensify the fiscal squeeze, forcing more aggressive cost control or deeper service reductions.
findings.figures: 3.59% forecast for 2026/27 vs 5.26% in 2024/25 and 4.63% in first six months of 2025/26
findings.quote: The investment performance for 2026/27 is therefore forecast at 3.59%. The average rate of return for 2024/25 was 5.26% and for the first six months of 2025/26 was 4.63%.

findings.headline: By 2028/29, the Council may need to borrow to finance day-to-day operating activity, not just capital schemes, if reserves continue to fall.
findings.detail: The liability benchmark shows that if reserve balances continue to decrease at the current rate, the Council will be forced to borrow for operational cash flow by 2028/29 in addition to borrowing for capital. This is a structural solvency risk indicator.
findings.matters: Borrowing for day-to-day operations rather than capital investment signals that the Council cannot balance its revenue budget and has reached a critical point in its financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Risk emerges by 2028/29 if current trajectory continues
findings.quote: The benchmark also suggests that if reserve balances continue to decrease as currently anticipated, then the Council may need to borrow to finance day-to-day activity in addition to its capital programme by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Treasury management costs are rising by £2.7m in 2026/27, with further increases forecast in future years as capital programme borrowing grows.
findings.detail: The budget for treasury management (MRP and interest on borrowing) is increasing by £2.7m in 2026/27. The report notes that further increases will be required in future years due to the increasing costs of capital programme borrowing, compounding the revenue budget pressure.
findings.matters: Structural growth in debt-servicing costs crowds out discretionary spending and signals that the Council's revenue budget is being consumed by interest and principal repayment rather than service delivery.
findings.figures: £2.7m increase to Treasury Management budget in 2026/27
findings.quote: It is proposed that an increase of £2.7m is made to the Treasury Management budget in 2026/27 due to the current falling interest rate environment and reducing investments. With interest rates expected to normalise at a lower level in the medium term, alongside increasing costs of capital programme borrowing, it is modelled that further increases to the budget will be required in future years.

findings.headline: Cash balances are falling and reserves are being used to bridge the budget deficit, with no end point visible in the MTFP forecast.
findings.detail: Reserves have declined in 2025/26 due to planned use, revenue budget overspend, and debt maturities. The Council expects cash balances to fall further in 2026/27 due to forecast deficit spending. The deficit position persists through to 2028/29.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce the Council's buffer against unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls and typically precede either service cuts or unsustainable borrowing escalation.
findings.figures: Cash balances falling further in 2026/27; deficit forecast to 2028/29
findings.quote: Cash balances are expected to reduce further into 2026/27 due to the Council's forecast deficit position and borrowing need.

findings.headline: Total borrowing need is £121m over three years, with external borrowing required from 2026/27 as cash reserves deplete.
findings.detail: The Council will need £121m in total borrowing (£51m for capital programmes, £70m from capitalisation direction). External borrowing is expected to begin in 2026/27 rather than being met from reserves. Internal borrowing capacity has been reduced from £75m to £50m, further increasing external borrowing need.
findings.matters: Escalating external borrowing and shrinking internal reserves indicate reduced financial flexibility and increased dependence on capital markets, raising refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £121m total borrowing over 2026/27–2028/29; £51m capital, £70m capitalisation direction; internal borrowing reduced from £75m to £50m
findings.quote: The total level of borrowing need over the next three years (between 2026/27 and 2028/29) is estimated to be £121m, split as £51m capital programme borrowing between 2026/27 and 2028/29 and £70m capitalisation direction in 2026/27.

findings.headline: East Sussex has applied for Exceptional Financial Support to treat revenue spending as capital, suggesting acute financial stress.
findings.detail: The Council faces structural financial challenges and has requested permission from Government to reclassify certain revenue expenditure as capital, allowing it to be funded by borrowing instead of the revenue budget. This capitalisation direction is for £70m in 2026/27 alone, indicating the Council cannot absorb these costs from operating revenue.
findings.matters: Seeking exceptional financial support is a formal signal that normal budget adjustments are insufficient, flagging acute fiscal distress to lenders evaluating credit risk.
findings.figures: £70m capitalisation direction in 2026/27
findings.quote: the application to Government for Exceptional Financial Support (ESF) in the form of a capitalisation direction. This would allow the Council to treat certain types of revenue expenditure as capital expenditure, allowing them to be funded by borrowing or capital receipts as opposed to from the revenue budget.

findings.headline: Council is minimizing borrowing in face of 'increasingly challenging financial position' driven by unmatched demand growth
findings.detail: The council explicitly states its plans reflect an 'increasingly challenging financial position' caused by growth in statutory demand-led services for vulnerable children and adults, escalation of costs, and national funding not meeting new costs. It is seeking to minimize borrowing to reduce pressures on Treasury Management.
findings.matters: Demand-led service growth (children's and adults' social care) is the hardest cost to control. If statutory spending is outpacing funding, this will eventually force either further service cuts or budget deficits that cannot be solved by capital programme adjustments.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The plans and budget reflect the increasingly challenging financial position facing the Council. This is due to the growth in need for statutory, demand-led, services for vulnerable children and adults, an escalation of costs, and national support and funding not meeting the new costs facing the authority.

findings.headline: Council has limited asset base available to generate capital receipts
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies a 'limited asset base' and notes it must prioritise use of capital receipts for short-life assets (IT equipment) rather than major infrastructure in order to minimize the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) cost of long-life assets. This suggests limited scope to unlock capital through asset sales.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a key non-borrowing funding source. If the asset base is limited, the council has fewer options to fund capital without borrowing, and may be forced to defer critical maintenance.
findings.figures: Commercial property portfolio valued at £12.1m (31 March 2023) with annual net income of £0.3m (2022/23)
findings.quote: Due to a limited asset base and significant levels of borrowing in the programme, the Council will continue to prioritise capital receipts to offset borrowing within the programme.

findings.headline: Treasury Management revenue budget capacity is diminishing and expected to cease as borrowing requirements increase
findings.detail: The council currently holds capacity in its treasury revenue budget (for contingencies, slippage, and investment returns) but explicitly expects this to erode over time as capital programme borrowing grows. This limits its ability to absorb shocks or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Eroding treasury headroom means less financial flexibility for a council already cutting capital programmes. When contingency capacity runs out, the council will have no buffer for overspends or interest rate movements.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The Treasury Management revenue budget currently holds capacity due to the following items, but it is anticipated that this capacity will dimmish and cease over time as the need to borrow to finance the capital programme increases.

findings.headline: Council actively cutting capital investment to reduce borrowing costs due to structural revenue pressures
findings.detail: The council has modified its capital programme specifically to reduce the impact of borrowing on revenue budget. This followed a 2024 RPPR review that proposed cutting core council-funded programmes. The driver is growth in statutory demand-led services (vulnerable children and adults) combined with escalating costs that are outpacing national funding increases.
findings.matters: Active capital programme cuts signal revenue budget strain that borrowing cannot hide. A lender needs to know whether this council is choosing to defer investment prudently, or whether it is forced to do so.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document; referred to as changes made in November 2024 RPPR
findings.quote: In order to reduce the cost of borrowing the Reconciling Policy, Performance and Resources (RPPR) report update on planning for 2025/26, reported to Cabinet in November 2024, proposed changes to the capital programme outside of normal Capital Strategy updates. The purpose was to reduce the level of investment in core council funded programmes and reduce the impact of borrowing on the Council's revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual VFM Report on ESCC 2024-25
findings.headline: Council must develop savings plans to bring its cost profile 'as lean as it can be'
findings.detail: The auditor's key recommendation is that the Council continue to develop savings plans, explicitly naming efficiency and service changes as routes to savings. The recommendation implies these are ongoing efforts and that further work is needed to achieve a sustainable cost profile while providing statutory services.
findings.matters: The need for continued significant savings development signals structural overspend or capacity problems that require substantive service or operational changes to resolve.
findings.figures: No specific savings target or timeline given in this summary
findings.quote: Savings plans should continue to be developed, to identify savings, via efficiency, and/or changes in services, to ensure the cost profile of the Council is as lean as it can be, whilst providing the statutory services required.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual VFM Report on ESCC 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor continues to report significant red weakness in Financial Sustainability
findings.detail: Grant Thornton explicitly identifies and continues to report a significant "red" weakness regarding the Council's financial sustainability. This is the auditor's independent assessment of the Council's ability to maintain its arrangements and financial viability given the challenging operating environment local government faces.
findings.matters: An external auditor's identification of a significant financial sustainability weakness is the kind of independent assessment that materially affects creditworthiness and borrowing capacity.

findings.quote: GT continue to report a significant "red" weakness with regard to Financial Sustainability.

news_drafts.headline: East Sussex pension fund auditor finds £6.2m valuation difference left unadjusted; note corrected by £26.1m
news_drafts.lead:
East Sussex's external auditor has identified a net understatement of about £6.2m (£6,168k) in the pension fund's Level 3 investments at 31 March 2026, which management is not proposing to adjust. The investments carry a balance of £1.15bn. The fund's total net assets in the final accounts are £5.28bn. The figures are in Appendix 1 to the Pension Board's papers for 6 November 2026.

The difference arose from timing: investment managers updated their valuations after the draft accounts were circulated. Management proposes leaving the financial statements unchanged. In the paper's words, "Management are proposing not to amend the financial statements on the basis that the differences are not material both quantitatively and qualitatively." The Audit Committee is to confirm this through the Letter of Representation.

The auditor also found that Note 26 to the accounts disclosed outstanding capital commitments of £246.2m, against an independently verified total of £220.1m, a difference of £26.1m. The auditor found the disclosed figure was an output error that did not match the supporting workings, treated the difference as non-trivial and recommended the note be updated. Management agreed to amend it.

news_drafts.headline: East Sussex asks government for up to £70m of exceptional support to cover a £55.6m 2026/27 deficit
news_drafts.lead:
East Sussex County Council has asked the government for permission to capitalise up to £70m of its spending to balance this year's budget, which carries a £55.6m deficit. The request, set out in the strategic risk register put to Cabinet on 29 September 2026, is for exceptional financial support (EFS): permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and a last resort. The government has agreed in principle.

The papers set out the terms. The support covers one financial year only and must be paid back. The council says it has told the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) that, without further government funding to address the underlying challenges, it is likely to need the support again for 2027/28 "to deliver our statutory duties". The register puts the cumulative deficit at £117.7m by 2028/29.

The risk register states the position in the council's own words: "Our revenue budget for 2026/27 includes a £55.6m deficit, which has led us to request Exceptional Financial Support from Government." Revenue budget here means the day-to-day running costs of services, as opposed to spending on things that last. The papers give no further breakdown of the deficit in the material reported here.
